docs.title: What Is a Human Being?
docs.subtitle: Body and soul, the image of God, and what we are made of, with each serious view stated by its own best defenders
docs.question: When you look in the mirror, what exactly are you looking at? Are you a body with a soul tucked inside it, a kind of ghost driving a machine? Are you simply a body, a living physical creature with no separate part that floats free when you die? Or are you something stranger and more unified than either picture, a single living whole where soul and body are not two stacked things but one mystery? And when you die, before the resurrection, is there a you that is awake and with the Lord? Or do you sleep until the trumpet sounds? Almost every believer has stood at a graveside and wondered where the person went. This debate lives inside that question.

docs.title: Why the Apocrypha Is Disputed
docs.subtitle: The books between the testaments, and why Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant Bibles are different sizes.
docs.question: Pick up a Catholic Bible and you will find seven books a Protestant Bible lacks, Tobit, Judith, Wisdom of Solomon, Sirach, Baruch, and 1 and 2 Maccabees, along with longer forms of Esther and Daniel. An Orthodox Bible carries those and more, 1 Esdras, 3 Maccabees, the Prayer of Manasseh, Psalm 151. Protestants call these books the Apocrypha, hidden things. Catholics call the seven deuterocanonical, belonging to a second stage of canonical recognition. The Orthodox call them anagignoskomena, things that are read. They were written by Jews, mostly between roughly 300 before Christ and the first century, mostly preserved in Greek. They circulated inside the Greek Bible the early church used. The question is whether they are Scripture. Each communion has answered with its whole history. The answers do not agree.

docs.title: Who Is Jesus?
docs.subtitle: The one person in two natures, fully God and fully man. Every view the early church considered is stated in its own best voice before the church judged it
docs.question:
When you pray to Jesus, who are you praying to? A great teacher who showed us how to live? An angel or a half-god, the highest creature God ever made? God wearing a human costume that was not really flesh? Or something stranger and harder than any of these, a single person who is at the same time completely God and completely man? He got tired and wept and bled. And He forgave sins, stilled storms, and rose from the dead. The whole faith leans its weight on the answer. Christology is just the long word for asking, with care, exactly who Jesus is.

The Gospels do not hand us a tidy definition. They hand us a man who slept in a boat in a storm (Mark 4:38) and then stood up and told the wind to be quiet, and it obeyed Him. They show Him weeping at a tomb (John 11:35) and then calling the dead man out of it. They show Him hungry in the wilderness and then feeding thousands from almost nothing. The earliest believers prayed to Him, sang to Him, and were baptized into His name, and most of them were Jews who had been taught from childhood that there is one God and that worship belongs to Him alone. Something had broken their categories. They were not confused. They had met someone who did not fit the boxes they had, and they spent the next four centuries trying to find words large enough and exact enough to say what they had seen.

So the question is not a parlor game for theologians with time on their hands. It is the question every reader of the New Testament eventually has to answer. If Jesus is only a man, then His promises to forgive your sins and raise you from the dead are the promises of someone who cannot keep them. If He is only God and never truly one of us, then He never stood where you stand and His life is a beautiful display that touches nothing in you. The church kept asking the question because the answer decides whether the gospel is good news or a misunderstanding. Who is Jesus is the first question and the last one.

docs.title: The Church and the State
docs.subtitle: Five traditions on how the people of God relate to the governing power — two kingdoms, transformation, witness, the two cities, and theonomy — for the believer trying to hold faith and citizenship at once.
docs.question: What is the relationship between the church and the state, between the people of God and the governing power under which they live? Political theology is the branch of Christian thought that asks it: how the two kingdoms, or the two cities, fit together; whether the believer's task is to reform the public order under Christ's lordship or to witness to it as an alternative community; what obedience the state may rightly command and where that obedience must stop. You cannot settle it with a single verse, because Scripture holds Romans 13, which calls the ruler God's servant, in the same canon as Revelation 13, which unveils the ruler as a beast. The whole tradition is an attempt to hold both.

docs.title: What Is the Church?
docs.subtitle: Three traditions on the nature, government, and sacraments of the people Christ calls his own, written for someone who just walked in the door.
docs.question: What is the church, who rules it under Christ, and what happens at the water and the table? The word for this whole subject is ecclesiology, the doctrine of the church, from the Greek word for an assembly that has been called together. You cannot answer it by reading one verse. You have to ask what Christ founded, how he meant it to be ordered, and what he was doing when he gave his people two signs to keep.

docs.title: How the Whole Story Fits
docs.subtitle: Four faithful ways Christians read the Bible as one story that ends at Christ. And what hangs on the differences.
docs.question: Is the Bible one story or many? And if it is one story, what holds the pieces together as it moves from Adam to Abraham to Moses to David to Jesus and finally to the church? When God made promises to Israel about land and offspring and blessing, are those promises fulfilled in the church, still owed to national Israel, or somehow both? The frameworks below are not four religions. They are four ways of answering one question. How does the whole story fit?

docs.title: Creation and Providence
docs.subtitle: How and when God made the world, and how he holds it together now.
docs.question: When you confess that God made the heavens and the earth, you are saying something every Christian agrees on. But how did he do it, and when. Were the days of Genesis 1 ordinary twenty-four hour days, and is the earth a few thousand years old. Or is the earth billions of years old, with those days standing for long ages. Did God shape each creature directly, or did he work through the slow process that scientists call evolution. And is Genesis 1 even trying to answer those questions, or is it telling us something else entirely. This entry walks through four ways faithful Christians have answered, and tries to show each one at its strongest.

docs.title: The Attributes of God
docs.subtitle: Aseity, simplicity, omniscience, omnipresence, omnipotence, immutability, goodness. Classical theism, and the questions pressed against it.
docs.question: When Scripture says God is, what kind of being is being claimed. Not a very large, very old, very powerful version of us, a man writ cosmic. The God of the Bible is of a different order entirely. He depends on nothing, exists from himself, knows all that can be known. He is present everywhere without being contained anywhere. He can do all that power can do. He does not change in his being or character, and he is good without measure and without shadow. The classical tradition gathered these into a set of perfections and gave them names. Aseity, that God is from himself. Simplicity, that God is not composed of parts. Omniscience, omnipresence, omnipotence. Immutability, that God does not change. And the moral perfections, that God is holy, just, faithful, and good. The question this page asks is what each of these means, how strongly the tradition meant them, and where the hardest pressure falls. Because each perfection, pushed, raises a real question. If God cannot change, can he love, respond, grieve. If God knows everything, am I free. If God can do anything, why is there evil. The attributes are not a list to memorize. They are a portrait. And the portrait has edges that have been argued over for centuries.

docs.title: Does God Change His Mind?
docs.subtitle: Classical theism, open theism, and Molinism. Three accounts of how God's knowledge and human freedom fit together.
docs.question: The Bible says two things that are hard to hold at once. It says God knows the end from the beginning, declares what is to come before it happens, and has numbered your days before one of them began. And it says God responds. Abraham bargains with God and God yields. Moses intercedes and God relents. Hezekiah prays and God adds fifteen years to his life. Nineveh repents and God does not send the disaster he announced. So which is it. Did God always know exactly what would happen, including every free choice you will ever make, so that the relenting is only apparent. A way of speaking. Or does God genuinely respond, adjust, and even change course in real partnership with creatures whose choices are not yet settled. And underneath that lies the oldest knot in theology. If God already knows, infallibly, what you will choose tomorrow, in what sense is the choice yours. And could you do otherwise. Three serious answers have been worked out, each defended by careful believers, each trying to keep both God's greatness and our freedom without sacrificing either. None of them is comfortable. Each pays a price somewhere.

docs.title: Who Is God? The Trinity
docs.subtitle: The one God who has always lived as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and why the church staked its life on getting this right.
docs.question: When a Christian says the word God, who is being named? Is God a single solitary person who later appeared in different forms, or three separate gods working together, or something the words barely stretch to hold: one God, undivided, who has eternally existed as three who love one another?

docs.title: The Holy Spirit and His Gifts
docs.subtitle: On the one Spirit all Christians confess, and the live question of whether the miraculous gifts continue today.
docs.question: The Holy Spirit is fully God, the third person of the Trinity. He convicts the world of sin, regenerates the dead heart, indwells every believer, and sanctifies the people of God over a lifetime. Christians do not argue over any of that. The live question is narrower and sharper. Did the miraculous gifts, also called the sign gifts, gifts like speaking in tongues, prophecy, healing, and the working of miracles, continue past the first generation of the church? Or did they cease once the apostles had finished their work and the Scriptures were complete? Faithful believers who love the same Bible answer that question in three different ways.

docs.title: Does God Suffer?
docs.subtitle: Classical impassibility, passibilism, and the qualified middle. Three accounts of whether God can be moved by our pain.
docs.question: When your world falls apart, and you cry out to God, what is happening on his side. Does your pain reach him. Does he feel it. The Bible seems to say yes without hesitation: God is grieved, God is moved with compassion, God's heart recoils within him, and at the center of the faith stands a cross where God in Christ bleeds. And yet the church for most of its history confessed that God is impassible, that he does not suffer, is not overcome by passions, is not made to ache by anything outside himself. That sounds, at first, like a contradiction or a cruelty. So the question is sharp and personal. Is the God you pray to in your worst hour a fellow sufferer who weeps with you, or an unmoved fullness whose love is steadier than any feeling. Or is the truth some careful third thing the tradition was reaching for all along. And what did the church mean by impassibility. It was never, in its best forms, the claim that God is cold. The dispute is not whether God loves. It is what kind of love a perfect, infinite, unchanging God has, and whether that love can be wounded.

docs.title: Inerrancy and Its Spectrum
docs.subtitle: The Chicago Statement, infallibility, and limited inerrancy. What the battle for the Bible was actually about.
docs.question: Inerrancy is the claim that Scripture, in everything it affirms, is without error. That includes its statements about history and the world, not only faith and morals. Infallibility, as its advocates use the word, is the claim that Scripture will never fail or deceive in what it was given to teach, the way home to God. Its incidental details speak the ordinary language of their time. Limited inerrancy splits the difference with a scalpel. Inerrant in everything revelational, everything that matters for doctrine and salvation. Humanly fallible in the incidentals. All three camps say the Bible is true. The question is what the word true is doing. And whether a Bible that could err about the small things you can check can still be trusted about the large things you cannot.

docs.title: What Inspired Means
docs.subtitle: Dictation, verbal-plenary, dynamic, and encounter. Four accounts of how the breath of God became human words.
docs.question: Paul writes that all Scripture is theopneustos, breathed out by God. Peter writes that men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit. Both verses state a fact and neither explains a mechanism. So how did it work. When Jeremiah dictated to Baruch, when Luke interviewed eyewitnesses, when Paul wrote a letter with greetings and a request for his cloak, what was God doing. And what were the men doing. Did God supply the very words. Did He supply the message and let the men find the words. Did He prepare the men so thoroughly that their free words were His words. Or is the Bible the human witness to revelation, the place where God reliably meets us, rather than a book whose sentences are themselves divine speech. Four serious answers have been given. Each one is trying to protect something the others can lose.

docs.title: How Does It End?
docs.subtitle: Eschatology, the study of the last things, and why the Christian hope holds steady even where sincere believers read the timeline differently.
docs.question:
Eschatology is the part of Christian teaching that deals with the last things, from the Greek word eschatos, meaning last. It asks how the story of the world ends. Scripture answers the heart of that question with one voice. Christ will return in person. The dead will be raised in their bodies. There will be a final judgment. God will make a new creation, a renewed heaven and earth where he dwells with his people and every wrong is set right. A new believer can rest the whole weight of their hope on those four things. The ancient creeds confess them. The Apostles Creed says he will come to judge the living and the dead. The Nicene Creed adds that his kingdom will have no end. The church has always held these together, across every century and every continent, before anyone drew a single chart.

The contested question is narrower. It sits underneath those shared truths rather than over them. Revelation chapter 20 speaks of a thousand years, a period often called the millennium, from the Latin mille and annus, meaning thousand and year. During this time the great enemy is bound and the souls of the faithful reign with Christ. Where does that thousand years fit on the timeline? Is it the present age of the church, stretching from the resurrection to the return? Is it a future earthly reign that Christ sets up when he comes back? Is the number a literal count on a calendar, or is it a symbol of fullness, the way other numbers function across the rest of Revelation? And underneath even that question sits an older one, the question of how to read apocalyptic writing at all, whether the visions of John move in strict chronological order or circle the same events from different angles.

These are the questions that have produced the four main positions you will meet below. They turn on the order of the resurrection in Revelation 20, on whether the binding of Satan describes something already accomplished or still to come, on what God still owes the nation of Israel, and on whether the church is removed from the great tribulation or carried through it. None of these is the question of whether Christ returns. That is settled. This is the real argument of this entry, and it is a family argument, not a battle line.

docs.title: How to Use This Section
docs.subtitle: Before the doctrines, the ground rules. How to read fairly, where the lines actually fall, and what I am trying to do here.

docs.title: Do Miracles Still Happen?
docs.subtitle: Cessationist, continuationist, and open-but-cautious accounts of the miraculous in God's providence, and Hume's old objection.
docs.question: A church gathers around a dying woman and prays for healing. Does anyone in the room expect God to actually do it. And what do they think happened if she lives, or if she dies. That is the question of this page. It is older and broader than any debate about spiritual gifts. Does God still pierce the ordinary course of nature with the extraordinary, the unmistakable sign, the healing medicine cannot explain, the deliverance that bends the laws He Himself set running. The Bible is full of such acts. But they cluster, around the Exodus, around the prophets, around Jesus and the apostles. And they run thin in the long stretches between. So is the age of obvious miracles essentially closed, a foundation laid once for all to authenticate revelation. Is it open and ongoing, the same Spirit doing the same works wherever faith and need meet Him. Or is the honest answer a watchful middle, God free to do the extraordinary, His people right to ask, and wise to weigh every claim soberly. And underneath it all sits the skeptic's old challenge. A miracle is by definition the least likely thing, and so never the most reasonable thing to believe.

docs.title: How We Got the New Testament
docs.subtitle: The criteria, the Muratorian fragment, Athanasius in 367, and what Nicaea never decided.
docs.question: Within a generation of the crucifixion, Christian communities possessed letters of Paul, and within two generations they had written Gospels. By the late second century, lists were being drawn. In 367, bishop Athanasius of Alexandria circulated an Easter letter naming exactly our twenty-seven books, the first surviving document to do so. Councils at Hippo in 393 and Carthage in 397 affirmed the same list. The historical sequence is reasonably clear. The question underneath it is not. When the early church sorted Matthew from the Gospel of Thomas, was it conferring authority or recognizing it. Did the books become canon when the church listed them. Or were they canon from the day they were written, with the lists merely catching up. And what do the slow cases tell us about how God gives a Bible to a church. Hebrews was doubted in the West. Revelation was doubted in the East. 2 Peter was doubted nearly everywhere for a time.

docs.title: The Origins Debate
docs.subtitle: Four Christian readings of Genesis 1 and 2, each in its own strongest voice. Young-earth, old-earth, evolutionary creation, and the framework view.
docs.question: Genesis opens with a claim no other ancient book makes plainly. One God, with no rival and no raw material, spoke everything into being and called it good. That much the whole church confesses. The argument is about the next layer down. Genesis 1 sets the work in six days and rests on the seventh. Is it telling us the duration of creation, the age of the world, the order of events as a camera would record them. Or is it doing something else with the days, something an ancient reader would have caught and a modern reader trained on science can miss. How old is the earth. Does it matter to the text. What is the relationship between Adam, formed from dust in Genesis 2, and the long history of life that the rocks and the genomes seem to record. Four serious Christian answers have been given. Each one reads the same two chapters, confesses the same Creator, and struggles honestly with something the others find easier.

docs.title: How We Got the Old Testament
docs.subtitle: When the Hebrew canon closed, who says so, and how you would know.
docs.question: Your Old Testament has thirty-nine books. The Hebrew Bible has the same books counted as twenty-four, arranged in three divisions, the Law, the Prophets, and the Writings. Nobody disputes that by the second century of the Christian era, Jewish communities held a defined collection they regarded as sacred Scripture. The question is when that definition happened. And what kind of event it was. Was the canon substantially closed early, by the time of Ezra or at latest the second century before Christ. So that Jesus inherited a settled Bible. Or did the third division, the Writings, stay soft at the edges into the first and second centuries after Christ, with books like Esther, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs still under discussion in the rabbinic schools. And either way, who had the authority to say, and does the church receive the list from the synagogue or know it through her own life with God.

docs.title: The Problem of Evil
docs.subtitle: Why this question breaks faith. The logical problem, the evidential problem, and an honest account of the weight.
docs.question: A child dies slowly of a disease no one chose. A good man is tortured by men who go unpunished. An earthquake buries a city that did nothing to deserve it. And the Christian says God is good, and God is all-powerful, and God is in control. Hold those three claims next to the dying child and the question writes itself, the oldest and hardest in the world. If God is good, he would want to stop it. If God is all-powerful, he could stop it. It is not stopped. So either he is not as good as you say, or not as powerful as you say, or not there at all. Epicurus is supposed to have framed it that way more than two thousand years ago. Nothing has dulled it since. This is not a puzzle for seminar rooms. It is the question that empties pews, the one whispered in hospital corridors, the one that has taken more people out of the faith than every clever atheist argument combined. And there are really two versions of it. One tries to prove the Christian God impossible. The other simply asks whether, given all this suffering, belief in him is reasonable. The first can be answered. The second cannot be dismissed. This page takes both seriously. It refuses the cheap comfort that has done so much harm.

docs.title: Providence
docs.subtitle: How God governs all things. Concurrence, primary and secondary causes, and the Reformed, Arminian, and Molinist accounts of his rule.
docs.question:
When a sparrow falls, when a lot is cast and lands, when wicked men crucify the Lord of glory and God means it for salvation, what exactly is God doing. The Bible says He works all things according to the counsel of His will, that He numbers the hairs of your head, that not a sparrow falls apart from the Father. It also holds people fully responsible for their choices, calls them to repent, grieves over their sin, and never once excuses a sinner on the ground that God decreed it. So how does God's complete government of the world relate to the real causes inside it, the weather, the human will, the free decisions that history is made of. Does He cause everything directly, work through secondary causes, permit what He hates, or somehow know and use the free choices His creatures would make. The doctrine of providence is the church's attempt to say how the King runs His world. The great traditions answer the how differently while confessing the that together.

The word itself carries the question. Providence comes from providere, to see ahead and to provide. But the church has never meant bare foresight. It means a governing care that reaches every creature and every event, what the older divines divided into preservation (God upholding all that exists from one moment to the next), concurrence (God working in and through the actions of His creatures), and government (God directing all things toward His appointed ends). The dispute on this page is not over preservation, which all confess, but over concurrence and government, the precise place where the divine cause and the creaturely cause meet. Aquinas located God as the first cause working through real secondary causes, so that to deny the creature its causality would, he argued, detract from the power of the Creator rather than honor it. Calvin pressed the rule of God down to the smallest detail and called bare foreknowledge a frigid notion next to it. Luis de Molina, writing in 1588, proposed that God knows what every free creature would do in any circumstance and governs by means of that knowledge. Open theists in our own time have asked whether the future of free choices is even there to be known in advance. Each of these is a different answer to one question. How can it be wholly true at once that God works all things and that the sinner, not God, is the author of his sin. Scripture asserts both without strain and rarely stops to explain how. The traditions on this page are the church reasoning carefully in the space between the two assertions.

docs.title: How God Speaks
docs.subtitle: General and special revelation, and how far the heavens can take you without a word.
docs.question: Christians have always said that God reveals Himself in two ways. General revelation is what God makes known to everyone everywhere through the created world, the moral sense, and the shape of human life. No Bible required. Special revelation is what God makes known by speaking, through prophets and apostles, through Scripture, and finally through His Son. Nobody in this debate denies that both exist. The question is what the first kind can actually do. Can an honest person reason from the world up to God, so that the arguments work and unbelief is a failure of logic. Or does sin so bend the human mind that the world's witness is always received and always suppressed, real enough to leave us without excuse but never enough to save. Or is the whole project of climbing from nature to God a mistake from the first step, because God is known only where He gives Himself, in Jesus Christ.

docs.title: The Sacraments: Baptism and the Lord's Supper
docs.subtitle: The two signs Christ commanded His church to keep. Who baptism is for, what happens at the Table, and why churches that share one Lord have never shared one answer.
docs.question:
On the night He was betrayed, Jesus took bread. Before He ascended, He commanded His church to make disciples and baptize them. Two acts, water and bread and wine, and there is no Christian tradition on earth that does not practice them in some form. The questions this page takes up are the two the church has never stopped arguing. Who is baptism for, the person who professes faith, or also the children of those who do? And what happens at the Table, is Christ present in the bread, with it, through it, or remembered by it? Even the name is contested. Sacrament comes from sacramentum, the Latin word for a soldier's oath of allegiance, the word the old Latin Bible chose to render the Greek mysterion. Ordinance is the word many Baptists prefer, an act ordained by Christ, chosen partly to guard against the idea that the rite works on its own. The word you reach for already leans toward an answer, which is a warning about how deep the disagreement runs.

The practices themselves are as old as anything we can see. The Didache, a church manual usually dated somewhere between roughly AD 50 and 120, gives instructions for baptizing in running water, allows pouring water on the head three times if no living water can be found, and restricts the Eucharist to the baptized. Justin Martyr, writing his First Apology in Rome around 155, describes the baptism of those who are persuaded and believe, and says of the bread and cup that we do not receive these as common bread and common drink. Both signs, then, from the church's first generations, and already carrying more weight than mere custom. But the early evidence does not settle the later disputes. The Didache never tells us whether the households being baptized included infants. Justin's reverence does not come with a metaphysics attached. The controversies came later, and when they came, they came hard.

The hardest of them can be dated. In October 1529, at Philip of Hesse's castle in Marburg, Martin Luther and Huldrych Zwingli met to unite the Reformation. They agreed on fourteen of fifteen articles, on Scripture, on the Trinity, on justification by faith, on nearly everything two reformers could be asked. The fifteenth article was the Supper. The story has come down that Luther wrote hoc est corpus meum, this is my body, in chalk on the table in front of him and would not move from it. Zwingli held that is meant signifies, as it plainly does when Jesus says I am the door. Witnesses report that Luther told the Swiss they had a different spirit. The colloquy failed, the Reformation divided at its own family meal, and the division has never healed. This page walks through what each tradition actually claims, at its strongest, and asks how a church is supposed to hold two signs its Lord commanded when His people cannot agree on what they are.

docs.title: What Is the Bible, and Can We Trust It?
docs.subtitle: Three faithful answers to the question of how Scripture is true.
docs.question: When a Christian says the Bible is true, what is being claimed. Is the claim that every sentence is exactly accurate, the way a modern reference book would be. Even its remarks about the age of a city or the order of an event. Or is the claim that the Bible never fails to deliver what God gave it to deliver, while it speaks in the ordinary words of ordinary people in the ancient world. Behind that lies a deeper question still. Where does the Bible's authority come from, and how are we meant to read it so that we hear God and not merely ourselves.

docs.title: Sin and the Fall
docs.subtitle: Original sin and how far the damage reaches. Three faithful traditions, each given its own strongest voice.
docs.question:
When the first man turned away from God in the garden, what exactly did the rest of us inherit. A wounded nature that pulls us toward wrong. The legal guilt of his act, charged to our account before we draw a breath. Only death and a broken world we are born into. The Bible says we are all caught in something that started before us, but it does not spell out the wiring in a single tidy sentence. So the church has read the same passages and reached three honest answers.

The question is older than the labels we now hang on it. It came to a head in the early fifth century, when a British monk named Pelagius taught in Rome that human beings are born morally neutral, able to keep God's commands by the unaided strength of the will, and that Adam's sin harmed no one but Adam by way of a bad example. Augustine of Hippo answered that the harm runs in the blood of the race, that we are born already turned away and unable to turn back without grace. The church sided with Augustine against Pelagius at the Council of Carthage in 418 and again, more carefully, at the Second Council of Orange in 529, which condemned the idea that we can take the first step toward God on our own. Those councils settled that we are fallen and cannot save ourselves. They did not settle the exact mechanism by which Adam's fall reaches each of us, and that is the unsettled ground the three views below still work.

Notice what the dispute is and is not. No faithful tradition says we arrive clean and merely pick up bad habits later. That is the Pelagian road the whole church closed. The live question is narrower and more precise. Do we inherit Adam's corruption only, the disordered nature, or do we also inherit his guilt, the legal verdict for his act, reckoned to us before we have done anything at all. And underneath even that lies a question about death itself, whether what came down to us is first of all a courtroom sentence or first of all a wound, a mortality that then breeds the sins each of us commits. Three traditions, reading the same Genesis and the same Romans, weigh those words differently.

docs.title: How Are We Saved?
docs.subtitle: Grace, election, and the human will, with each serious view stated by its own best defenders
docs.question: When a person is saved, who does what, and in what order? Does God choose us before we could choose anything, and then work in us the very willingness by which we come? Or does God offer grace widely and genuinely, and then wait on a free human yes that He has made possible but does not compel? When you came to faith, were you the one who reached out across the dark toward a God you had begun to want, or were you the one who had already been found and carried before you understood what was happening to you? The whole debate sits inside that single experience nearly every believer has had, the experience of looking back at your own conversion and not being able to say with certainty whether you found God or God found you. This is not a new question. It runs from Augustine arguing with Pelagius in the early fifth century, through the medieval schoolmen, into the Reformation and the long quarrel between the followers of Calvin and the followers of Arminius after the Synod of Dort in 1618 and 1619, and it continues in living churches today. The question matters because it touches the most intimate thing about you, the moment grace became real, and it asks who was the actor in that moment and who was the one acted upon.

docs.title: Sovereignty and Human Freedom
docs.subtitle: Compatibilism, libertarian freedom, and Molinism. Three accounts of how God's rule and the human will can both be real.
docs.question: Scripture never once apologizes for holding two things together that human logic strains to hold. God works all things according to His will. And you are fully responsible for what you do. It commands you to choose, warns you, pleads with you, and judges you, treating your choices as really yours. It also says God turns the king's heart, grants repentance, opens the heart to believe, and works in you to will and to act. So what is human freedom. Is it the power, at the moment of choosing, to have done otherwise, an open future genuinely up to you. Or is it acting according to your own strongest desire, uncoerced, even though God ordains what that desire will be. Or is there a third thing, a freedom God knows so exhaustively that He can sovereignly weave it into His plan without overriding it. The answer you give decides what you think happens in the deepest moment of human life. That is the moment a person turns to God or away from Him.

docs.title: Can We Trust the Manuscripts?
docs.subtitle: Textual criticism for beginners. The variants honestly counted, and what they do and do not touch.
docs.question: No original manuscript of any biblical book survives. What survives is copies, of copies, of copies. Roughly 5,800 catalogued Greek manuscripts of the New Testament in whole or part. Some ten thousand more in Latin, thousands more in Coptic, Syriac, and other languages, plus the biblical quotations that saturate the church fathers. No two manuscripts agree exactly. The differences between them are called variants, and the best current estimates put the total around half a million. Textual criticism is the discipline that compares the copies to establish, as nearly as possible, the original wording. The question of this page is the one your neighbor asks on the porch. With no originals and half a million variants, can you honestly claim to know what the New Testament said. And inside the church, a second question: by what method, and from which manuscripts, should we decide.

docs.title: Theodicies Steelmanned
docs.subtitle: The free-will defense, soul-making, skeptical theism, and the cross-centered and protest responses. Each at its strongest.
docs.question: Grant that the existence of God and the existence of evil are not flatly contradictory, that the logical problem can be answered. A harder question remains. Can we say anything, even tentatively, about why a good and all-powerful God permits the suffering we see. Can we at least show that he might have a reason worth the cost. A theodicy is an attempt to do exactly that, to justify the ways of God in the face of evil. Over the centuries several have been built, each serious, each defended by careful minds. The free-will defense says the great good of genuine freedom required the possibility of its abuse. The soul-making theodicy says a world with suffering is the only kind that can grow real souls. Skeptical theism says we are in no position to judge whether God has good reasons we cannot see. And a different kind of response, the cross-centered and the protest traditions, says the whole project of explanation is a mistake. The right answer to evil is not a theory but a God who suffers and a lament that refuses to make peace with the horror. This page lays each out at its strongest, with the author hidden, and asks which, if any, can carry the weight. The test is not only whether an answer is logically sound. It is whether it can be said out loud at a graveside without becoming a lie.

docs.title: Why Translations Differ
docs.subtitle: Word for word, thought for thought, and paraphrase. What each philosophy protects, and how to choose without fear.
docs.question: Hold two Bibles side by side at Psalm 23 or Romans 3 and the wording differs, sometimes slightly, sometimes startlingly. Why. A small part of the answer is textual, treated on the manuscripts page of this set. The large part is translational philosophy. Hebrew and Greek are not English. Every sentence forces choices between keeping the form of the original, its word order, its idioms, its ambiguities, and conveying the sense of the original in natural English. Formal equivalence leans toward the form: the NASB, ESV, and KJV. Functional equivalence, also called dynamic, leans toward the sense: the NIV moderately, the NLT thoroughly. Paraphrase sits past the far end: The Message renders Scripture in contemporary idiom with maximal freedom. Which philosophy best serves the reader, and which Bible should you actually use, is the question. The three schools answer it with conviction.

docs.title: The Trinity: One God, Three Persons
docs.subtitle: The biblical data, the four centuries the church spent working it out, and the one live debate that remains.
docs.question:
The first Christians were Jews who would have died before calling anyone but the Lord their God. The Shema was the daily prayer pressed into them from childhood. Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one. They did not abandon that confession. They never thought of themselves as having left it. And then these same hardened monotheists prayed to Jesus. They baptized in his name. They called him Lord in the sense the Old Testament reserved for the unspeakable Name, the kyrios who is the God of Israel. They sang to him as to a god, a Roman governor noticed by the early second century. They spoke of the Spirit as God too, the Spirit who searches the deep things of God and whom no creature could search. And yet they did not think they had three Gods. They did not think Father, Son, and Spirit were three masks one actor wears in turn. So what had they seen. What was forced on them by the resurrection and by the coming of the Spirit at Pentecost that made faithful Jews speak this way without believing they had broken the first commandment.

That is the question this doctrine answers. How can the God who is one be Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, each fully God, each truly distinct from the others. Without three Gods. Without dissolving the three back into one. The early church did not reach the answer quickly or cleanly. It took almost three hundred years, from the apostolic writings through the Council of Nicaea in 325 and the Council of Constantinople in 381, with bitter conflict, imperial interference, and exiles in between. Tertullian had already given the Latin West the language of one substance and three persons around the year 200. The East worked toward its own grammar through Origen, through the long crisis Arius set off, through Athanasius and then the Cappadocians. The point was never to produce a riddle that clever people could solve. The point was to confess rightly what God had revealed and to guard that confession against the ways it kept getting broken. The words the church settled on, one being in three persons, eternally begotten, of one substance, were not speculation. Each was chosen against a specific way of getting God wrong, and each marks the place where an earlier teacher had gone over a cliff.
